C001.name: Extended reality
C001.definition: Extended reality (XR) refers to extending reality by some means. Systematically, it involves using systems to either augment our reality or replace our perception of reality.

C002.name: Virtual reality
C002.definition: Virtual reality (VR) is a specific type of immersive experience mentioned in the course title. It involves creating a simulated environment that users can interact with.

C003.name: Augmented reality
C003.definition: Augmented reality (AR) is another specific type of immersive experience mentioned in the course title. It involves overlaying digital information onto the real world.

C004.name: Mixed reality
C004.definition: Mixed reality (MR) is a distinct term that is currently being heard in the field. It represents a specific type of reality blending.

C005.name: Immersive technology
C005.definition: Immersive technology is a type of technology where the user experiences an environment through sensory organs in such a way that they fail to distinguish it from the real environment. This perceived experience leads the user to assume the environment is real.

C006.name: Reality-virtuality continuum
C006.definition: Reality-virtuality continuum is a scale used to visualize the spectrum between a completely real environment and a completely virtual environment.

C007.name: Virtual environment
C007.definition: Virtual environment is one extreme of the scale where there is nothing real present, meaning the environment is completely virtual.

C008.name: Augmented virtuality
C008.definition: Augmented virtuality is the opposite of augmented reality, where a virtual world is enhanced by incorporating real-world content.

C009.name: Metaverse
C009.definition: The Metaverse is not merely an application of virtual reality, mixed reality, or augmented reality technology. The Metaverse is a broad concept that involves reimagining how humans interact with the digital world in an all-around 3D environment.

C010.name: Human-computer interaction
C010.definition: Human-computer interaction is a different way of looking at how humans interact with digital content. This interaction occurs within a 3D environment using a natural way of interaction.

C011.name: Cognitive side
C011.definition: Cognitive side refers to the understanding of the human mind that is necessary to grasp how our senses influence the desired experience when using technology or a system.

C012.name: Psychological side
C012.definition: Psychological side refers to the understanding of the human mind that is necessary to grasp how our senses influence the desired experience when using technology or a system.

C013.name: Interactions
C013.definition: Interactions refers to the process of designing and implementing how users engage with the environment within VR or AR systems.

C014.name: Virtual tours
C014.definition: Virtual tours are experiences that allow a user to visit a place remotely, even if they cannot physically go there. This method saves both money and physical effort for the user.

C015.name: Heritage tourism
C015.definition: Heritage tourism involves allowing users to explore a heritage place virtually, even if physical visits are restricted. This enables users to explore every part of the heritage space without having to travel there.

C016.name: Preservation of digital heritage
C016.definition: Preservation of digital heritage is the process of digitally saving a heritage space, often in the form of virtual tours. This digital preservation can increase the lifespan and potential for the space to be visited by many users.

C017.name: Non-immersive
C017.definition: Non-immersive refers to a virtual experience obtained through a computer where the user controls activities within the software, but the environment does not directly interact with the user. This type of system relies on psychological engagement, allowing the user to remain physically attached to, a

C018.name: Augmentation
C018.definition: Augmentation is the process of enhancing the real world by overlaying digital content onto it. This focus is distinct from Virtual Reality, which emphasizes a fully simulated environment.

C019.name: Immersive experience
C019.definition: Immersive experience is a concept emphasized in Virtual Reality (VR) where the user is fully enveloped in a simulated environment. This level of immersion is not a mandatory requirement for Augmented Reality (AR).

C020.name: Telemedicine
C020.definition: Telemedicine is an application that enables medical professionals to interact with patients remotely. It is one of the many interesting applications developed using Augmented Reality.

C021.name: Virtual tape measure
C021.definition: Virtual tape measure is an augmented reality application that allows users to measure heights or lengths of objects. This tool eliminates the need for carrying a physical tape measure.

C022.name: Markerless AR application
C022.definition: Markerless AR application is a versatile type of AR that does not require placing any markers in the physical world. These applications function based on computer vision techniques, allowing users to decide where virtual objects are placed.

C023.name: Holographic projection
C023.definition: Holographic projection is an example of a projection-based technique. This technique can be utilized in the development of Augmented Reality (AR) applications.

C024.name: Marker-based
C024.definition: Marker-based systems are easier to create and rely on simple algorithms. However, these systems require a very sanitized environment to maintain the markers, as they are prone to damage in outdoor settings.

C025.name: Markerless
C025.definition: Markerless techniques are used to overcome the maintenance difficulties of markers. These techniques primarily rely on computer vision and may utilize other sensors, such as GPS sensors, for location-based applications.

C026.name: Fully immersive
C026.definition: Fully immersive is one of the three categories of Virtual Reality (VR) systems. This category is defined by the importance of the psychological aspect and the overall experience provided to the user.

C027.name: Superimposition-based
C027.definition: Superimposition-based is a type of computer vision-based application. This application involves placing digital content over the real-world view.

C028.name: Artificial environment
C028.definition: Artificial environment is a computer-generated setting that is not real, which must be populated with artificial objects. This environment can be a graphical representation of either a real world or an imaginary world.

C029.name: Sensory stimuli
C029.definition: Sensory stimuli are computer-generated inputs that a VR system provides to the user. These stimuli allow the user to experience the artificial or synthetic environment through their sensory organs, such as their eyes and ears.

C030.name: Interactivity
C030.definition: Interactivity is the characteristic of a VR system where dynamic changes in the virtual environment occur based on the user's actions or inputs. This allows the user to interact with the elements present in the environment, similar to how they interact with objects in the real world.

C031.name: Non-immersive VR
C031.definition: Non-immersive VR is a screen-based experience that does not meet the criteria for a fully immersive experience. This type of experience is sometimes called regular computer screen based experience.

C032.name: Superimposition
C032.definition: Superimposition is a category of AR system where extra information is placed over the building space. This allows digital content to appear on the real-world view.

C033.name: Phases
C033.definition: Phases are distinct periods into which the evolution of the field can be divided, although some overlap may occur between them.

C034.name: Stereoscopic device
C034.definition: Stereoscopic device is a type of apparatus that allows the brain to interpret two-dimensional images as three-dimensional objects. This device established the possibility of creating a sense of depth from flat images.

C035.name: Stereoscopic vision
C035.definition: Stereoscopic vision is the biological ability of the brain to perceive three-dimensional space by viewing two-dimensional images. This perception allows us to see images together as objects existing in 3D space.

C036.name: Flight simulator
C036.definition: Flight simulator is an early concept developed to provide an immersive experience. It utilizes multiple sensors to simulate the environment, serving as a precursor to modern multi-sensory VR experiences.

C037.name: Head-mounted display
C037.definition: Head-mounted display is a new kind of computer display that people began working on in the 1950s. It is a device worn by the user to display visual information.

C038.name: Haptic feedback
C038.definition: Haptic feedback is a method where touch sensations are provided to the user. This allows the user to feel objects on the screen while manipulating them.

C039.name: CAVE system
C039.definition: CAVE system is a type of immersive environment that used a single computer to render images in a surrounding setting, giving the user the sensation of being surrounded by holograms.

C040.name: WTK package
C040.definition: WTK package is a software package developed in 1992 that provided higher-level tools for application development within Virtual Reality (VR).

C041.name: Virtual Reality Modeling Language
C041.definition: VRML is a modeling language for virtual reality that was presented in 1994, which subsequently led to the appearance of many other modeling languages.

C042.name: Field of view
C042.definition: Field of view is a technical specification, such as the 150-degree FOV, that describes the angular extent of the visual area presented by a Head-Mounted Display (HMD).

C043.name: Growth phase
C043.definition: Growth phase is the last and continuing phase of VR evolution, which began around 2016. This phase is characterized by continuous development and acceleration of the field.

C044.name: Developmental phase
C044.definition: Developmental phase is one of the four evolutionary stages used to describe the history of VR. These phases track the evolution of the technology over time.

C045.name: Experimental phase
C045.definition: Experimental phase is the initial period of development that occurred before the 1980s. This phase was primarily related to early experimentation, which defined concepts and showed the types of technology required.

C046.name: Tools or applications phase
C046.definition: Tools or applications phase is the period spanning from the mid-1990s to 2007. During this phase, early applications and exploratory tasks were developed, focusing on interaction techniques, usability, and design theory related to AR.

C047.name: Commercial application phase
C047.definition: Commercial application phase is the current phase, starting from 2007. This phase is characterized by widespread AR availability and the continuous emergence of newer applications in various market domains.

C048.name: Tracking
C048.definition: Tracking is the process used to register content in 3D, which allows people to see and interact with shared augmented reality content. This technology is specifically done to register the content in three dimensions.

C049.name: Head mounted display
C049.definition: Head mounted display is an optical see-through device that is worn by the user. This device is used to display augmented or virtual content onto the user's view.

C050.name: Computer-generated imagery
C050.definition: Computer-generated imagery is graphics created by a computer that can appear either superimposed over the real world view or as a substitute for the real world view. This imagery is used to augment or replace the user's perception.

C051.name: Prototype AR system
C051.definition: Prototype AR system is an early functional system that combined an optical see-through head mounted display with a ceiling-mounted mechanical tracking system and custom graphics hardware. This system was designed to register 3D content based on head movements.

C052.name: Registration tracking techniques
C052.definition: Registration tracking techniques were research areas carried out during the early development of the field. These techniques helped in the overall development of the field.

C053.name: See-through head mounted displays
C053.definition: See-through head mounted displays were utilized in early research on AR during the period of 1995 and 1996. These displays allowed for the development of AR applications.

C054.name: AR interaction methods
C054.definition: AR interaction methods refer to the ways in which a user can interact with the augmented digital content. Work was carried out on these methods in 1993.

C055.name: Mobile AR systems
C055.definition: Mobile AR systems were a topic of research carried out during the basic research phase. These systems were developed alongside other AR research activities.

C056.name: Viewpoint tracking
C056.definition: Viewpoint tracking is the activity of determining how to track the user's viewpoint. This is necessary so that the registration of content in 3D happens accurately.

C057.name: Wearable computing
C057.definition: Wearable computing refers to devices, such as headsets, where the computer hardware is carried externally, for example in a backpack. Interaction with these devices is achieved through different input devices.

C058.name: AR overlay on real-world marker
C058.definition: AR overlay on real-world marker is a technique that uses computer vision to place augmented reality content onto physical markers in the real world.

C059.name: Commercial phase
C059.definition: Commercial phase is the stage of AR evolution where AR experiences transition from niche research to becoming widely popular and available to the general public. This phase is characterized by increased commercial interest and the potential for AR applications to drive sales and popularity of goods.

C060.name: AR authoring tools
C060.definition: AR authoring tools are software that enable the creation of Augmented Reality experiences. These tools, such as those based on Adobe Flash, made it possible to experience AR directly through web browsers, thus expanding accessibility.

C061.name: ARKit SDK
C061.definition: ARKit SDK is a Software Development Kit launched by Apple for the purpose of developing Augmented Reality systems. This launch significantly stimulated growth in the field by allowing a large number of developers to create AR applications.

C062.name: Tracking and registration in 3D
C062.definition: Tracking and registration in 3D is the process of accurately locating and mapping objects within a three-dimensional space. This capability is expected to become increasingly feasible on low-end devices due to advancements in AI and computer vision.

C063.name: Defining characteristic
C063.definition: Defining characteristics are features that help distinguish between different types of systems. These characteristics allow one to differentiate between a virtual reality system and an augmented reality system, for example.

C064.name: Virtual reality system
C064.definition: Virtual reality system is an artificial environment that is experienced through sensory stimuli. This environment is provided by a computer and allows the user's actions to partially determine what happens within it.

C065.name: Technological issue
C065.definition: Technological issue refers to the challenge of generating suitable stimuli for a virtual environment. This involves figuring out how to create the necessary inputs for the user to experience the virtual world.

C066.name: Psychological issue
C066.definition: Psychological issue refers to the challenge of how a user perceives the stimuli that have been generated. This relates to the human factor and how individual psychological characteristics affect perception.

C067.name: Sensory organs
C067.definition: Sensory organs are the biological mechanisms that are activated in a suitable way to receive input. Activation of one or more sensory organs is what technology can do to generate an immersive experience.

C068.name: Immersion
C068.definition: Immersion is the objective or technological experience provided by a system. Immersion aids the potential for a user to feel present in a virtual world.

C069.name: Extensive
C069.definition: Extensive refers to the range of sensory modalities that are presented to the user. The more sensory organs that are stimulated by the stimuli provided by the computer, the more extensive the immersion is.

C070.name: Matching
C070.definition: Matching refers to the congruence between different sensory modalities. For instance, the visual presentation must instantly correspond to head motion and the virtual representation of the user's body.

C071.name: Surrounding
C071.definition: Surrounding is the extent to which the cues provided are panoramic. This refers to the scope of the field of view for visual senses or the extent of auditory perception for sound sources.

C072.name: Vivid
C072.definition: Vivid is the quality of energy stimulated within a particular sensory modality. This quality relates to how much energy the computer generates to stimulate a sensory organ, which is enhanced by factors such as resolution, lighting, and audio bitrate.

C073.name: Presence
C073.definition: Presence is the subjective experience of feeling truly located within a virtual world. Presence is achieved when a user is unable to distinguish between the real world and the virtual world.

C074.name: Representational fidelity
C074.definition: Representational fidelity is the degree to which the VR experience conveys a place that is or could be on Earth. This fidelity measures how closely the VR experience matches or exploits the familiarity of a real-world place.

C075.name: Experiential fidelity
C075.definition: Experiential fidelity is the degree to which the user's personal experience matches the intended experience of the VR creator. Higher experiential fidelity is achieved when real-world constraints are incorporated into the virtual world's navigation, movement, and interaction.

C076.name: Immersion
C076.definition: Immersion is a concept tied to the technological issues of Virtual Reality (VR) systems. It relates to the technological aspects of the VR experience.

C077.name: Pose
C077.definition: Pose refers to the viewer's position and orientation within the context of the system. Pose determination is necessary to register virtual content in the real world.

C078.name: Registration phase
C078.definition: Registration phase determines the pose of a viewer relative to a real world anchor. This phase is performed when the user begins using the system.

C079.name: Tracking phase
C079.definition: Tracking phase is the process that follows registration, requiring the continuous updating of the viewer's pose relative to a previously known pose. This is necessary because the user is likely to move while using the AR application.

C080.name: Real world anchor
C080.definition: Real world anchor is a physical element in the environment used by the system to anchor virtual content. This allows the virtual content to appear as a seamless part of the physical environment.

C081.name: Uncanny valley effect
C081.definition: The uncanny valley effect is a phenomenon where making environments familiar to the user can sometimes lead to feelings of uneasiness or creepiness. This occurs even when the objective is to make the environment as familiar as possible to the user's real-world experience.

C082.name: Cyber sickness
C082.definition: Cyber sickness is a major concern related to VR systems that will be discussed in detail. The discussion will cover its causes, how it can be measured, and strategies to reduce or eliminate it.

C083.name: Mitigation
C083.definition: Mitigation refers to the strategies that can be adopted to overcome the challenges associated with cybersickness. Finding a feasible solution to reduce the impact of cybersickness is extremely important in the context of VR systems.

C084.name: Evaluation
C084.definition: Evaluation refers to the process of measuring or assessing cybersickness. This process helps determine how to know if cybersickness has happened or is going to happen.

C085.name: Causes
C085.definition: Causes refers to the factors that can lead to cybersickness. It is important to understand that not a single factor is responsible for this condition.

C086.name: Motion sickness susceptibility
C086.definition: Motion sickness susceptibility is an internal factor referring to an individual's tendency to experience motion sickness. This susceptibility is related to Cyber sickness because both conditions involve the brain receiving conflicting sensory signals.

C087.name: Body awareness
C087.definition: Body awareness is the ability of the user to attend to and perceive bodily sensations. This awareness can be affected by factors such as poor sleep quality.

C088.name: Inter-pupillary distance
C088.definition: Inter-pupillary distance (IPD) is the distance between the user's pupils. This distance determines how stereoscopic vision is achieved through the HMDs.

C089.name: Display resolution
C089.definition: Display resolution is a hardware factor that determines the clarity of the visual experience. Higher resolution generally leads to a better experience and reduced cybersickness up to a specific point.

C090.name: Latency
C090.definition: Latency is the time gap between an action performed in the physical world and the corresponding change reflected in the virtual world. Increased latency is found to increase the likelihood of inducing sickness.

C091.name: Latency jitter
C091.definition: Latency jitter is the variability in the time gap between a user's action and its reflection in the virtual world. This variability causes irregularities in the timing of data delivery, leading to discomfort and disorientation.

C092.name: Type of display
C092.definition: Type of display is a hardware factor that significantly influences the severity of cybersickness symptoms. Users utilizing Head-Mounted Displays (HMDs) tend to feel more cyber sick compared to those using conventional monitors.

C093.name: Type of input
C093.definition: Type of input refers to the various methods used in virtual reality, such as hand controllers or treadmills. The specific input device or technology used can cause cybersickness to vary.

C094.name: Visual motion
C094.definition: Visual motion stimulus is the movement experienced by the user within a virtual environment. This stimulus is considered one of the primary causes of cyber sickness, and its severity is affected by how the content moves.

C095.name: Vection
C095.definition: Vection is the sensation of self-motion, which is the feeling of movement experienced by the user. This sensation is highest when the user perceives motion in peripheral stimuli.

C096.name: Means of locomotion
C096.definition: Means of locomotion refers to how a user is moving within the virtual world. This aspect of movement affects cyber sickness because a mismatch between virtual and physical movements can cause disorientation.

C097.name: Questionnaire-based input
C097.definition: Questionnaire-based input is a method of input where users rate their discomfort or disorientation using self-report scales. These scales are typically administered before, during, or after the experience.

C098.name: Physiological input
C098.definition: Physiological input is an objective method used to detect cybersickness by measuring bodily functions. Examples of these inputs include heart rate, galvanic skin response, and EEG.

C099.name: Behavioral input
C099.definition: Behavioral input involves detecting cybersickness using observable cues related to how a user moves. These cues include head and body movement, blink rate, and postural sway.

C100.name: Content-based input
C100.definition: Content-based input measures cybersickness by analyzing features within the virtual reality environment itself. These features include optical flow and depth cues.

C101.name: Simulator Sickness Questionnaire
C101.definition: Simulator Sickness Questionnaire (SSQ) is a widely used questionnaire designed to measure cybersickness. It contains 16 items divided into subscales for oculomotor, disorientation, and nausea symptoms.

C102.name: Manual evaluation
C102.definition: Manual evaluation is a measurement technique that relies on human intervention to assess cyber sickness. This process requires someone to distribute questionnaires, collect feedback, and analyze responses to determine the severity or onset of cyber sickness.

C103.name: Automated evaluation
C103.definition: Automated evaluation is a measurement technique that uses automated algorithms to measure cyber sickness. This method processes various inputs, such as physiological or biometric data, to automatically determine the presence of cyber sickness.

C104.name: Transparent models
C104.definition: Transparent models are types of models that provide clear insight into their internal workings and decision-making process. When an automated evaluation uses these models, the process is easily understood.

C105.name: Stepwise regression analysis
C105.definition: Stepwise regression analysis is a method utilized to measure cyber sickness using a variety of physiological signals. This technique is considered to be a transparent model.
